title: Builder and Prototype
goal: By the end you can choose between named arguments, a Java record with a builder, and a Kotlin DSL builder, and make copies of templates that never share changeable parts with the original.
opening:
At the town's sandwich counter, nobody orders by reciting eight words in a fixed order. You say "rye bread", then "cheese", then "no onions", and the person behind the counter adds each part as you go. At the end they check that it really is a sandwich, with bread and a filling, and hand it over finished. Down the street, the print shop has a photocopier. Fill in a form once, copy it, change two lines on each copy, and you've saved an hour.

Objects with many optional parts have the same two needs. A constructor with seven parameters is a sandwich ordered in one breath, and nobody can tell which `true` meant "fragile". And a copy that changes two fields is so handy that it's easy to miss what it didn't copy.

In the last lesson, factories decided which class to make. In this lesson, we'll decide how to make one object with many parts: Kotlin's named and default arguments, a Java record with a builder, a Kotlin DSL for nested orders, and copies that never share what they shouldn't. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.

warmup.q: `data class Cart(val id: String, val items: MutableList<String>)`. You run `val c2 = c1.copy(id = "c2")` and then `c2.items += "milk"`. What happens to `c1.items`?
options: It now contains `milk` too, because both carts share one list
It throws, because data class properties can't change
It depends on whether `c1` was declared with `val`
warmup.why: `copy()` is shallow. It copies the reference to the list, not the list, so `c1` and `c2` hold the same `MutableList`. `val` only stops you from pointing the property at another list; it says nothing about what's inside the list. Java records behave the same way. The last section of this lesson takes it apart and fixes it.

sections.h: Prototype: every copy is shallow until you make it safe
sections.body:
Now the photocopier. **Prototype** means making a new object by copying an existing one and changing a few fields. The shop does this every week: the Saturday breakfast box is set up once, and each customer gets a copy with their own name and notes. Tests do it too, with one sample order copied and changed in each test.

Java's original tool for this, `Cloneable`, is broken by design. The interface has no `clone` method, so implementing it gives callers nothing to call. `Object.clone()` is protected, and it makes a shallow copy (more on that in a moment). To use it, you override `clone`, call `super.clone()`, catch a `CloneNotSupportedException` that can't happen, and then fix every changeable field by hand. Skip it. Use a copy constructor, a static copy factory, or a wither on a record.

Records make withers easy to write, and Kotlin data classes generate `copy()`. Neither copies deeply. The Kotlin docs say it plainly: `copy()` creates a shallow copy, and references to other objects are shared. A **shallow copy** copies each field's value, and when the value is a reference to another object, such as a list, it copies the reference, not the list:

```kotlin
data class Cart(val id: String, val items: MutableList<String>)
val c1 = Cart("c1", mutableListOf("bread"))
val c2 = c1.copy(id = "c2")
c2.items += "milk"          // c1.items is now [bread, milk]
```

```java
record Cart(String id, List<String> items) {
    Cart withId(String newId) { return new Cart(newId, items); }   // a wither: shares the list
}
var c1 = new Cart("c1", new ArrayList<>(List.of("bread")));
var c2 = c1.withId("c2");
c2.items().add("milk");     // c1.items() is now [bread, milk]
```

That was the warm-up. `copy()` is very obliging: it copies exactly what you asked for, the reference, and not one thing more. Here the photocopier picture breaks. A photocopy is a separate piece of paper, and writing on it never changes the original. But picture a form with a shopping list clipped to it. `copy()` gives you a new form with the same shopping list clipped on, so writing on the copy's list writes on the original's. The figure shows both carts holding one list.

The fix is the same in both languages. Store collections that can't change, `List.copyOf` in a compact constructor in Java and a read-only `List` in Kotlin, and let withers build a new collection: `copy(items = items + "milk")`. Then sharing is harmless, because nobody can write on the shared sheet.

**A copy is only as safe as the parts it shares. Share only parts that can't change.**

Kotlin has a second trap. `data class Email private constructor(val value: String)` still gets a public `copy()`, so `Email.of("anna@example.com").copy(value = "not-an-email")` compiles and skips your factory. Kotlin 2.4 only warns, at the line that calls `copy`:

```text
w: CopyTrap.kt:29:24 This 'copy()' exposes the non-public primary constructor of a 'data class'. ... This will become an error in language version 2.5.
```

Add `@ConsistentCopyVisibility` to make `copy()` as private as the constructor today. A check in an `init` block is safer still, because `copy()` runs it. Java records never had this illusion. A record's canonical constructor, the one that takes every component, can't be less visible than the record itself, so the rules belong in the compact constructor from the start.

Check yourself. The shop's breakfast box template is a data class with `val tags: MutableList<String>`. Anna's copy gets the tag `"no nuts"` through `annasBox.tags += "no nuts"`. What do Ben's box and the template now say? (Both say `no nuts` too, because all three share one list. With a read-only `List` and `copy(tags = tags + "no nuts")`, only Anna's box changes.)

compare.title: A prototype that copies safely

java.title: DeliveryPlan.java

kotlin.title: DeliveryPlan.kt
kotlin.src:
data class DeliveryPlan(
    val district: String,
    val days: List<String>,                    // read-only types
    val feeCents: Map<String, Long>,
)

val base = DeliveryPlan("town center", listOf("MON", "THU"), mapOf("BIKE" to 250L))
val harbour = base.copy(
    district = "harbour",
    days = base.days + "SAT",                  // + builds a new list
)

compare.note: Kotlin generates `copy()` with named arguments, so it needs no withers, and `+` on a read-only `List` or `Map` returns a new collection. Java needs one hand-written wither per field. Both copies are shallow, and the safety comes from the parts, not from the copy. There's one real difference. Java's compact constructor can replace the incoming list with `List.copyOf`, while a Kotlin data class property can't be reassigned in `init`. A Kotlin `List` parameter is only read-only, so a caller who passes a `MutableList` and keeps a reference to it can still change it. If that matters, take the list as a plain constructor parameter and store `toList()` in a property.

worked.title: From a telescoping constructor to a record and builder, and to a Kotlin class

steps.say: Here's the label call from the first section, with all seven arguments. Before reading on, say which argument is the note, and which rules you'd expect `Label` to enforce.
steps.code: new Label("12 Mill Lane", "Anna", true, true, false, 1, "ring twice");
steps.alt_code: Label("12 Mill Lane", "Anna", true, true, false, 1, "ring twice")

steps.say: Put every rule in one place that all paths go through: the record's compact constructor in Java, the `init` block in Kotlin. The rule that relates two fields (a this-way-up arrow only goes on a fragile label) can only be checked where all the fields are known. Kotlin also gets its defaults here, which is half of what a builder does.

Java needs a builder that only collects and supplies defaults. Its `build()` calls the record's constructor, so the rules run there. Kotlin needs no builder: named arguments do the job, and `@JvmOverloads` gives Java callers some overloads. If Java code calls the Kotlin class often, add a builder for it too.

lab.title: A checking order DSL, and a prototype that stops leaking
steps: Open the two files. `OrderDsl.kt` is the order DSL from this lesson, and `OrderTemplate` is the shop's prototype for regular orders such as the Saturday breakfast box.
Run the tests. Twelve of thirteen fail: the DSL is all `TODO`, and `OrderTemplate` leaks tags and notes between copies.
In `OrderDsl.kt`, write `ItemsBuilder`: keep a private `MutableList`, and return `toList()` from `build()`.

Write `OrderBuilder`: `items` runs the block on a fresh `ItemsBuilder` and keeps its items, `note` puts into a private map, and `build()` checks with `require` and copies the collections into the `Order`. Then write `order`. Put `@OrderDsl` on both builder classes.
Fix `OrderTemplate.java`: add a compact constructor that stores `List.copyOf` and `Map.copyOf`, and make the withers copy the collection, change the copy, and build a new template.
Run the tests until all thirteen pass.
hints: `require(condition) { "customer is required" }` throws `IllegalArgumentException` with that message when the condition is false.
`ItemsBuilder().apply(block).build()`: `apply` runs the lambda with the builder as `this` and returns the builder.
In a record's compact constructor, `tags = List.copyOf(tags);` replaces the parameter before the field is set. You don't write `this.tags = ...`.
lab.done_when: All thirteen tests in `OrderDslTest` and `OrderTemplateTest` pass.

alt.title: Java

recap: Kotlin's named and default arguments, plus `copy()`, replace most builders. Put the checks in `init`: it runs for every construction, `copy()` included.
A builder still helps for Java callers, for objects built over several steps, and for nested data. In Java, pair a checking record (its compact constructor) with a builder that only collects.
A type-safe DSL is a function that takes a lambda with receiver (`Builder.() -> Unit`). `@DslMarker` stops an inner block from quietly reaching an outer builder.
`Cloneable` has no `clone` method, and `Object.clone()` is shallow. Use copy constructors, copy factories or withers.
Record withers and data class `copy()` are shallow. Store collections that can't change, and build new collections in withers.

The limit: no copy in either language is deep, so a copy is only as safe as the parts it shares. And in Kotlin 2.4, a private constructor doesn't make `copy()` private without `@ConsistentCopyVisibility`.
closing:
We started at the sandwich counter and the photocopier. In code, named arguments let you order in one breath, and a builder still earns its place for Java callers and nested orders. Copies were the surprise: every `copy()` and wither shares whatever its fields point to.

Now look in your own code for a data class or record that holds a `MutableList`, a `HashMap` or an array, then search for its `copy(` or wither calls. Each may hand out a shared shopping list.

Next, we'll stop building our own objects and start fitting other people's. When an old program speaks a different language from ours, how do we use it without its words spreading through the shop?

quiz.q: `data class Fee(val cents: Int) { init { require(cents in 0..1_000) } }`. What does `Fee(250).copy(cents = 5_000)` do?
quiz.why: `copy()` calls the primary constructor with the new values, so every `init` block runs again and `require` throws. That's why `init` is the safest place for a data class's rules. What `copy()` does skip is a checking factory, when the constructor is private.

quiz.q: Java code will call your Kotlin `Label(address, name, fragile = false, thisWayUp = false, express = false, copies = 1)` constructor from many places. What helps that code most?
options: Add `@JvmOverloads`, or give Java a builder
quiz.why: Java has no named or default arguments, so it sees one six-parameter constructor. `@JvmOverloads` generates overloads that drop trailing defaults, and a builder lets Java code set any mix of fields by name. `@JvmStatic` applies to companion members, not constructors, and `data` changes nothing for Java callers here.

quiz.q: A DSL has no `@DslMarker`. Inside `items { }`, someone writes `currency = "USD"`. `ItemsBuilder` has no `currency`, but the outer `OrderBuilder` does. What happens?
quiz.why: Both receivers are in scope inside the inner lambda, so the compiler finds `currency` on the outer builder and sets it. Nothing fails. With `@DslMarker` on both builders, that line becomes a compile error unless you write `this@order.currency`.

quiz.q: `record Cart(String id, List<String> items) {}`. `c1` was built with `new ArrayList<>(List.of("bread"))`. Then `Cart c2 = new Cart("c2", c1.items()); c2.items().add("milk");`. What happens?
options: `c1` is unchanged, because records can't change
quiz.why: A record only stops its fields from pointing somewhere else. The `ArrayList` a field points to can still change, and `c2` shares it. A compact constructor with `items = List.copyOf(items);` would give each record its own unmodifiable list, and the `add` would then throw.

quiz.q: From *Factory Method and Abstract Factory*: you hide a data class's constructor (`data class Email private constructor(val value: String)`) and offer a checking `Email.of(raw)`. In Kotlin 2.4, which line still creates an unchecked `Email`?
options: None: a private constructor covers every path
quiz.why: The generated `copy()` stays public even when the constructor is private; Kotlin 2.4 only warns about it. So `copy` creates an `Email` your factory never saw. `@ConsistentCopyVisibility` makes `copy()` private, and a check in `init` would run on `copy()` too. A direct constructor call from outside doesn't compile.

flashcards.front: Does a Kotlin data class's `init` block run on `copy()`?
flashcards.back: Yes. `copy()` calls the primary constructor, so the `require` checks in `init` run again.

flashcards.front: What is a lambda with receiver?
flashcards.back: A function type like `Builder.() -> Unit`. Inside the lambda, `this` is the Builder, so you call its members without a prefix.
Calling a member of an outer DSL receiver without a prefix from inside an inner block. Reaching it then needs an explicit `this@label`.
It declares no `clone` method, and `Object.clone()` is protected, shallow and throws a checked exception. Use copy constructors or withers.

flashcards.front: Is a Kotlin data class `copy()` deep or shallow?
flashcards.back: Shallow. A property that holds a changeable object, such as a `MutableList`, is shared by the original and the copy.

flashcards.front: Where do the checks go for a Java record that has a builder?
flashcards.back: In the record's compact constructor, so `build()`, withers and direct `new` calls all run them.

flashcards.front: `data class Email private constructor(...)`: is its `copy()` private in Kotlin 2.4?
flashcards.back: No. It stays public, with a warning. Add `@ConsistentCopyVisibility` to make it private.

terms.plain: A chain of constructors, each adding one more optional parameter.
A helper that collects values step by step and makes the finished object in `build()`.
A lambda whose `this` is a given object, written `T.() -> R`.
An annotation for your DSL's own marker annotation; it limits calls without a prefix to the nearest receiver.
Making a new object by copying an existing one and changing a few fields.
A method like `withWindow(w)` that returns a copy with one field changed.
A copy that shares the objects its fields point to, instead of copying them too.

explain_back.prompt: A colleague says: "Kotlin data classes can't change, so `copy()` gives us safe, independent order templates." Explain where that's wrong, and how you'd make templates safe in Kotlin and in Java.
explain_back.answer: A data class is only as unchangeable as its properties. `val` stops a property from pointing somewhere else, but if it holds a `MutableList` or a `HashMap`, `copy()` copies the reference, so the template and every copy share that collection, and changing one changes all of them. To make templates safe, give them collections that can't change. In Kotlin, use read-only `List` and `Map` types, and `copy(tags = tags + x)` to build new ones. In Java, use a record whose compact constructor stores `List.copyOf` and `Map.copyOf`, and withers that copy, change the copy and construct a new record. I'd also put the rules in `init` or the compact constructor, because `copy()` and withers go through them.

deeper.body:
Effective Java's hierarchical builder solves a problem you may meet in a shared Java library: a `Pizza.Builder` that subclasses (`NyPizza.Builder`, `Calzone.Builder`) extend without losing the subclass's type in a chain of calls. It uses a recursive type parameter, `Builder<T extends Builder<T>>`, and an abstract `self()` method that each subclass implements as `return this;`. *Advanced generics: recursive bounds, T & Any, @UnsafeVariance* in the generics track showed why that recursive bound works. In Kotlin you almost never need it, because named arguments and `copy()` remove the chain.

Java has no `with` syntax for records yet. Project Amber, the OpenJDK project for smaller language features, has proposed one, derived record creation (JEP 468), where you would write something like `point with { x = 3; }`. Check its status on the JEP page before you plan around it. Until then, write withers for the fields that really change.

People sometimes copy a whole tree of objects deeply by turning it into bytes and back (serialization), or with a reflection library. It works, it's slow, and it copies things you didn't mean to copy, such as a shared clock or an open connection. If you need a deep copy, the cleaner fix is usually to make the parts unchangeable, so a shallow copy is enough.

Kotlin's `buildList { add(...) }`, `buildMap { }` and `buildString { }` are small standard-library builders with receivers. Use them when you build a collection with loops or conditions; the result is read-only once the block returns.
